newsitem.title: FINLAND: Finnish shares seen unfazed by ERM news.
newsitem.headline: Finnish shares seen unfazed by ERM news.

text.p: The only real surprise in Finland's move to link the markka to Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) this weekend was the timing, and business will be as usual on the Helsinki bourse on Monday, analysts said.

A rate of around 3.03 markka per German mark had been expected for the peg and was factored into prices, they said. If anything the link rate of 3.04 announced on Saturday was a slightly positive surprise.
"I think it is quite a reasonable level," said FIM Pankkiiriliike analyst Niklas Geust. "I don't think there will be any problems in competitiveness," he said.
The most important thing, particularly for the forest industry which is Finland's second largest exporter, is the level of the Swedish crown, he said.
"And it is clear that it is now even more important than before that productivity increases be taken into account in wage and wood purchase negotiations," Geust said.

Merita Pankkiiriliike forest industry analyst Anna-Maija Pirskanen said the 3.04 per mark rate was clearly below the industry's hopes which were closer to 3.20 than 3.10. But given the markka's recent strength, it was expected, she said.
She expected no immediate market reaction.
"We have to remember that this is only the central rate; there is also the fluctuation range," she noted.
"We have been tracking the U.S. market very closely recently. We will continue to move in the world's pace," she said.
The Confederation of Industry and Employers (TT) said in a statement after the ERM link that cost moderation would now be very important, in pay talks and in public finance and taxation.
But TT chief economist Jussi Mustonen said the 3.04 rate was better than the worst case scenario he had feared.
"Indeed it is clear that we prefer to have it this way -- they have taken into account a balanced exchange rate over a year."
"But this does mean that cost moderation is absolutely necessary, in wage negotiations as well as in public sector finances and taxation," Mustonen said.

But even without any immediate market reaction, the ERM peg may prove an important signal that Finland aims to be part of core Europe in creating monetary union and that may in the long run draw more investors to Finland, analysts said.
"In that sense it could have an impact," said FIM's Geust.
Handelsbanken Finland chief economist Carlo Erakallio said the fact that Finland now became one of the "EMU-likelies", instead of being just an "EMU-possible", may bring new funds to Finland.
"There could be a shift of portfolios from Sweden to Finland," he said.
